Class ADRCConfig

java.lang.Object
yams.core.math.ADRCConfig
All Implemented Interfaces:
Cloneable
public class ADRCConfig extends Object implements Cloneable
Configuration for an active disturbance rejection controller.

Written by FRC Team 8331, who contributed active disturbance rejection control to YAMS.

An active disturbance rejection controller lumps everything the mechanism model does not capture (friction, back-EMF, game-piece loads, dropped battery voltage, unmodeled dynamics) into a single "total disturbance" and estimates it live with an extended state observer. The estimate is then cancelled out of the control law, so the closed loop behaves like a clean chain of integrators that settles in the time you ask for, without hand-tuning gains. There is no proportional, integral, or derivative gain to tune: you describe the plant (order and input gain) and the response you want (settling time), and the controller derives its own gains.

This is the drop-in equivalent of withClosedLoopController(...): pass it to SmartMotorControllerConfig.withADRCController(ADRCConfig) and the motor controller runs the active disturbance rejection controller on its own closed-loop thread. Mechanisms need no extra code; they keep calling setVelocity(...) and setPosition(...) exactly as they would with a PIDController.

Getting started

Like every other YAMS config class, this is a plain builder: teams set the values they tune with the withX(...) methods, usually from their Constants class. A complete velocity-loop configuration for a shooter wheel looks like this: 

new ADRCConfig()
    .withSystemOrder(SystemOrder.FIRST)
    .withSettlingTime(Seconds.of(0.2))

Every value starts empty. The getters return that empty Optional, and buildController(DCMotor, SmartMotorControllerConfig, Time) fills it with the default documented on the withX(...) method. The one exception is systemOrder, which has no default: buildController(DCMotor, SmartMotorControllerConfig, Time) throws until it is set.

Choosing the system order

The system order is the number of integrators between the motor voltage and the quantity the closed loop commands and measures. Pick the lowest order that describes your loop; the observer adds one more state on top of the plant order, so higher orders are more sensitive to sensor noise.

  • ADRCConfig.SystemOrder.FIRST: you command and measure velocity (flywheels, shooter wheels, intake and conveyor rollers). A brushed or brushless DC motor's velocity responds to voltage directly, so most FRC speed loops are first order.
  • ADRCConfig.SystemOrder.SECOND: you command and measure position, and the mechanism's inertia sets how fast it moves. Position is the integral of velocity, which adds one order.
  • ADRCConfig.SystemOrder.POSITION, ADRCConfig.SystemOrder.ARM, ADRCConfig.SystemOrder.PIVOT and ADRCConfig.SystemOrder.ELEVATOR: you command and measure position, and the config chooses the form when the controller is built. A mechanism geared down far enough has its speed set by its motor's back-EMF more than by its inertia: each volt moves it at about the same speed, so its position is first order, with its speed per volt as b0. Otherwise its position is second order, with its acceleration per volt as b0. See ADRCConfig.SystemOrder.POSITION.
  • ADRCConfig.SystemOrder.THIRD and ADRCConfig.SystemOrder.FOURTH: rare. Use when the measured quantity sits two or more integrations behind the voltage, for example a mechanism whose actuator itself has significant first-order lag. Most mechanisms never need these.

Velocity loops and position loops differ only in the order; every other option in this class works the same for both.

Tuning the response

  • withSettlingTime(Time) sets how quickly the closed loop settles after a setpoint change. The default, 0.2 seconds, is a good starting point. Lower is faster and more aggressive but demands more voltage and stresses the mechanism; higher is gentler.
  • withBandwidthScale(double) scales both the closed-loop bandwidth and the observer bandwidth together. Above 1.0 is more aggressive, below 1.0 is more conservative. Leave it at the default of 1.0 until the settling time is dialed in.
  • withB0(double) sets the approximate input gain, meaning how strongly one volt accelerates the measured quantity. It only sets the controller's operating point, so being off by 20 to 50 percent usually still works. Leave it unset to derive it from the motor, gearing, and moment of inertia (see "What is never assumed" below); set it explicitly when the mechanism has no meaningful inertia, such as a mechanism driven against a hard stop.
  • withInputDelay(Time) compensates a known delay between commanding the output and seeing its effect, such as a deliberately slowed sensor. Zero (the default) disables it.
  • withCascaded(boolean) runs the observer in cascaded form, which some higher-order plants track more accurately. Leave it disabled unless you have a reason.

The output limits and ramp come from the motor config, as for every closed loop controller: withClosedLoopControllerMaximumVoltage(...) limits the output, and withClosedLoopRampRate(...) limits how quickly it changes.

The withX(...) methods only accept values the controller can use: an invalid one, such as a settling time that is not positive or a zero b0, throws IllegalArgumentException and leaves the config as it was. The controller reads its settings from this config instead of keeping copies, so the config never holds a value it cannot run.

Smoothing the reference with a tracking differentiator

A step setpoint asks the controller for an instantaneous change, which spikes the output and excites unmodeled dynamics. A tracking differentiator replaces the raw reference with a smoothed reference plus its derivatives, so the controller follows a feasible trajectory instead. Enable one with withTrackingDifferentiator(TrackingDifferentiator.Method, double...), for example: 

new ADRCConfig()
    .withSystemOrder(SystemOrder.FIRST)
    .withTrackingDifferentiator(TrackingDifferentiator.Method.LD, 0.08)

Five methods are available; see TrackingDifferentiator for the full parameter reference, and ADRCGuide.md for how to choose and tune one. Each entry below lists its parameters in order, in the loop's units (mechanism rotations, meters for a linear loop, or rotations per second for a velocity loop):

  • TrackingDifferentiator.Method.EULER, first-order exponential smoothing. One parameter, alpha in [0, 1] (default 0.9): higher is smoother and slower. The mildest option, but its yd jumps on a step.
  • TrackingDifferentiator.Method.TOD, time-optimal tracking. One parameter, r greater than 0 (default 1.0), the acceleration bound: higher tracks faster. Bang-bang, so yd chatters at rest at a 20 ms period.
  • TrackingDifferentiator.Method.LD, the linear differentiator. One parameter, lambda greater than 0 (default 1.0), a time constant in seconds; the sample period must be below 2 * lambda. No overshoot, and a step is followed in about 5.8 * lambda. The best default.
  • TrackingDifferentiator.Method.RED, the nonlinear differentiator. Two parameters, lambda1 and lambda2, both greater than 0 (default 1.0 each). A super-twisting filter that converges in finite time, but overshoots and chatters at a 20 ms period.
  • TrackingDifferentiator.Method.INTD, the integral differentiator. Four parameters: alpha in [0, 1) (default 0.5), and beta, gamma, r greater than 0 (default 1.0 each). Saturating: cruises at r * beta / (1 - alpha), then lands like LD; gamma = 4 * beta gives no overshoot.

Parameters may be omitted entirely to use the method defaults, and the differentiator is off by default. If the reference only ever ramps (a joystick-driven setpoint, for example), a differentiator buys little; it earns its keep on step changes.

What is never assumed

  • systemOrder must be set with withSystemOrder(SystemOrder). There is no safe default, so buildController(DCMotor, SmartMotorControllerConfig, Time) throws while it is unset.
  • b0 may be set with withB0(double). Otherwise it is derived from the motor, gearing, and the mechanism's moment of inertia, but only when the mechanism explicitly configured that inertia with withMomentOfInertia(...) or withWheelMomentOfInertia(...). The library's placeholder inertia is never used.
  • Output saturation comes from the motor config's withClosedLoopControllerMaximumVoltage(...), which the motor controller applies to every closed loop. The controller itself does not limit its output.
  • The control period comes from withClosedLoopControlPeriod(...), so the controller and the loop cannot disagree.

    • withBackEmfModel

      public ADRCConfig withBackEmfModel(boolean backEmfModel)
      Choose whether the observer models the motor's back-EMF. On by default.

      A motor's back-EMF brakes the mechanism in proportion to its speed. Left out of the observer's model, it is lumped into the disturbance the observer estimates, which then changes as fast as the speed does: the observer lags it whenever the mechanism speeds up or slows down, and a mechanism following a motion profile overshoots. Modeled, the disturbance only holds what the model misses, such as gravity and friction.

      Measured in simulation, a 12:1 pivot following a trapezoidal profile overshot by at most 1.1 degrees with it on the motor controllers simulated in step with the robot, and by up to 8.3 without, where the SPARKs oscillated. Held at a setpoint in a Pivot mechanism on a TalonFXS, whose simulation runs on CTRE's own real-time thread, it sometimes oscillated instead. To cancel the modeled back-EMF, the control law pushes with the observer's estimated speed, which cancels the damping the back-EMF gives the motor, so a loop whose timing is far from what it was built for can be better off without it.

      It applies to a position loop that chose second order when built from a motor config (see ADRCConfig.SystemOrder.POSITION), whose back-EMF time constant comes from the motor, the gearing and the moment of inertia. A first order position loop's b0, a speed per volt, already includes the back-EMF. A ADRCConfig.SystemOrder.FLYWHEEL still lumps it into the disturbance: modeled, a flywheel settled up to twice as fast at a settling time of 0.3 s or more, but overshot by up to 7% at 0.15 s on a loop with a period of delay. ADRCConfig.SystemOrder.FIRST to ADRCConfig.SystemOrder.FOURTH leave the model to you. Changing it on a built config works the gains out again.

      Parameters:
      backEmfModel - Whether to model the back-EMF.
      Returns:
      This config for chaining.

    • withTrackingDifferentiator

      public ADRCConfig withTrackingDifferentiator(TrackingDifferentiator.Method method, double... params)
      Enable a tracking differentiator on the reference. Disabled by default.

      The differentiator smooths the reference and supplies its derivatives, so a step setpoint no longer spikes the controller output. See the class documentation for a guide to the five methods and their parameters, and TrackingDifferentiator for the full reference.

      A motion profile on the motor config also shapes the setpoint, so a config with both is refused when the controller is built.

      Parameters:
      method - Differentiation method.
      params - Method parameters in order; leave them out to use the method defaults.
      Returns:
      This config for chaining.

    • buildController

      public ADRCController buildController(org.wpilib.math.system.DCMotor motor, SmartMotorControllerConfig<?> config, org.wpilib.units.measure.Time period)
      Build a controller from this config, filling every unset value with its default.

      The controller reads its settings from this config every step, and its gains too: the config keeps the control period, the b0 used while it is unset, and the gains worked out from them, and works the gains out again whenever its settling time, bandwidth scale or b0 changes. So a change, as live tuning makes, takes effect on the next step without resetting the state estimate. The system order, input delay and tracking differentiator only take effect when a controller is built, and a built config refuses a different order.

      The controller does not limit or ramp its output: the motor controller does, with withClosedLoopControllerMaximumVoltage(...) and withClosedLoopRampRate(...).

      Parameters:
      motor - Motor model used for b0 derivation.
      config - Motor config that carries gearing, inertia, circumference, and the loop period.
      period - Closed-loop control period.
      Returns:
      Initialized ADRCController.
      Throws:
      SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException - if the order is missing or b0 cannot be derived.
      SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException - if the config has a tracking differentiator and the motor config has a motion profile: both shape the setpoint.
      IllegalArgumentException - if ADRCController.initialize(double, Time) rejects the derived b0 or the tracking differentiator.

    • resolveB0

      public double resolveB0(org.wpilib.math.system.DCMotor motor, SmartMotorControllerConfig<?> config)
      Resolve the input gain: the one set, or one derived in the loop's units. For an ADRCConfig.SystemOrder.ELEVATOR it is the speed per volt, from the motor, gearing and mechanism circumference. Otherwise it is the acceleration per volt, derived only when the mechanism explicitly configured its inertia.
      Parameters:
      motor - Motor model.
      config - Motor config that carries gearing, inertia, and circumference.
      Returns:
      Input gain in the loop's units per volt per second to the plant's order.
      Throws:
      SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException - if the order is an elevator's and the closed loop is not linear, or b0 is not set and cannot be derived safely.
